title: Science: Food Chains and Fragile Land
objectives: I can explain how predators, prey, and decomposers connect in a food chain.
I can describe how erosion, pollution, and contamination change land and water.
I can use words like dwindle and flourish to describe changes in a habitat.
I can write a short science explanation using precise vocabulary.
rationale: This disciplinary unit gives fifth graders the vocabulary they need for life science and earth science. Three Tier 3 words (predator, prey, erosion) are named plainly and used in context, and the other seven words describe how living things and land are protected or harmed (pollute, contaminate, dwindle, flourish, decompose, fertile, nutrient). Students also use proof, trustworthy, and microscope from earlier units when they read and write about evidence.

words.def: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
words.ex: A hawk is a predator that spots mice from high above a field.
words.ex2: The wolf, a top predator, helps keep the number of deer in balance.
words.nonExample: A cow eating grass is not a predator.

apps.academic: In a food chain, a predator eats other animals to get energy.
apps.spoken: Owls are predators that hunt at night.
apps.writing: Use predator for an animal that hunts; the animal it hunts is its prey.

misuse.s: A rabbit is a predator that hunts and eats foxes.

words.def: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
words.ex: Small fish are prey for herons and otters.
words.ex2: A herd of zebras moves together so a lion cannot single out its prey.
words.nonExample: A hawk soaring over a field is hunting, so it is not the prey at that moment.

apps.academic: In an ecosystem, prey animals are food for predators.
apps.spoken: Rabbits are prey for many animals.
apps.writing: Use prey as a noun for the animal that is hunted for food.

cloze.s: The deer, a common ___ of wolves, kept its ears turned toward every sound in the forest.

cloze2.s: Camouflage helps a young fawn hide because it is ___ for many hungry animals.

misuse.s: The prey chased the hungry fox across the field to catch its dinner.
misuse.why: Prey is the animal being hunted; the fox is the hunter here.

visual.alt: A mouse watching an owl in a tree.

words.def: The slow wearing away of soil or rock by water, wind, or ice.
words.ex: Heavy rain caused erosion on the hillside, carrying soil into the creek.
words.ex2: Over millions of years, erosion by the river carved the Grand Canyon.
words.nonExample: A rock that stays whole for centuries has not suffered erosion.

apps.academic: Planting trees and grass can slow erosion on a steep slope.
apps.spoken: We saw erosion at the beach after the storm.
apps.writing: Use erosion for the slow movement of soil or rock caused by water, wind, or ice.

cloze.s: Farmers planted rows of trees along the field to stop ___ from carrying away the rich topsoil during storms.

cloze2.s: After years of waves hitting the cliff, ___ had worn a deep cave into its base.

misuse.s: Erosion is the process that adds a new layer of soil to the top of a hill.
misuse.why: Erosion wears soil and rock away; it does not add new layers.

visual.alt: Waves wearing away the base of a cliff.

words.def: Rich enough to grow many healthy plants.
words.ex: The river valley has fertile soil, so farmers grow corn and beans there.
words.ex2: Fertile fields near the delta produced enough rice for the whole region.
words.nonExample: Dry, rocky sand where nothing grows is not fertile.

apps.academic: Fertile land often forms where rivers leave behind rich soil.
apps.writing: Use fertile for soil or land that supports strong plant growth.

cloze.s: Corn grew tall and thick in the ___ soil of the river valley, where floods had left behind rich mud.

cloze2.s: Because the land was so ___, the farmers harvested twice as many pumpkins as last year.

misuse.s: Plants grow best in fertile soil that is hard, dry, and full of nothing.
misuse.why: Fertile soil is rich enough to grow plants; dry soil with nothing in it is not fertile.

visual.alt: A green seedling next to a field of grain.

words.def: To make something unsafe by adding harmful things to it.
words.ex: Spilled oil can contaminate a stream and harm the fish that live there.
words.ex2: Wash your hands so germs do not contaminate the food you are preparing.
words.nonExample: Adding clean water to a glass does not contaminate it.

apps.academic: Scientists test water to see whether harmful chemicals contaminate it.
apps.spoken: Don't let the raw chicken contaminate the salad.
apps.writing: Use contaminate when something harmful gets into food, water, soil, or air.

cloze.s: Leaking fuel from the old tank could ___ the well and make the family's drinking water unsafe.

cloze2.s: The lab worker wore gloves so that her fingers would not ___ the sample she was testing.

misuse.s: Adding fresh, clean water to a lake will contaminate it and make it unsafe.
misuse.why: To contaminate is to make something unsafe; adding clean water does not do that.

visual.alt: A barrel leaking into a drop of water.

words.def: To make air, water, or land dirty and harmful.
words.ex: Smoke from factories can pollute the air over a city.
words.ex2: The campers promised not to pollute the lake with soap or trash.
words.nonExample: Planting trees to clean the air does not pollute it.

apps.academic: Cars and factories can pollute the air unless they use cleaner fuels.
apps.spoken: Please do not pollute the river.
apps.writing: Use pollute for harm to a large part of the environment, such as air, water, or land.

cloze.s: Dumping trash and chemicals into the river would ___ the water that the town drinks.

cloze2.s: Engineers designed the new bus so that it would not ___ the air with thick black smoke.

misuse.s: Recycling paper and picking up litter will pollute the park.
misuse.why: To pollute is to make land dirty and harmful; picking up litter cleans it.

visual.alt: A factory sending smoke into the air.

words.def: To break down slowly into simpler parts, as dead plants do.
words.ex: Fallen leaves decompose on the forest floor and turn into soil.
words.ex2: In a compost bin, banana peels decompose in a few weeks.
words.nonExample: A glass bottle left on the ground does not decompose for a very long time.

apps.academic: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria help dead plants and animals break down.
apps.spoken: The apple core will decompose in the garden.
apps.writing: Use decompose for natural breakdown by living things such as fungi and bacteria.

cloze.s: Mushrooms and tiny bacteria help dead logs ___ into soft, crumbly soil.

cloze2.s: Because the cold slowed down the bacteria, the fallen apples took much longer to ___.

misuse.s: A plastic toy will decompose into rich soil in just one week.
misuse.why: Plastic does not break down quickly; to decompose is to break down into simpler parts, as dead leaves do.

visual.alt: Fallen leaves and a mushroom on the ground.

words.def: To become smaller or fewer little by little.
words.ex: As winter went on, the squirrel's store of acorns began to dwindle.
words.ex2: The pond's water dwindled during the summer drought until only mud remained.
words.nonExample: A river that rises after heavy rain is not dwindling.

apps.academic: When a habitat is lost, the number of animals in a region can dwindle.
apps.spoken: Our supply of paper is dwindling.
apps.writing: Use dwindle for a slow, steady drop in number or amount.

cloze.s: As more forest was cleared, the number of tree frogs began to ___ year after year.

cloze2.s: With each passing week of the drought, the town's water supply continued to ___.

misuse.s: The crowd at the fair dwindled as more and more people arrived.
misuse.why: Dwindle means to get smaller; more people arriving makes the crowd bigger.

visual.alt: A falling line on a graph beside a frog.

words.def: To grow well and be healthy and successful.
words.ex: Ferns flourish in the damp shade of the forest.
words.ex2: The little shop began to flourish after the neighbors told their friends.
words.nonExample: A plant with no sunlight or water will not flourish.

apps.academic: Coral reefs flourish in warm, clear, shallow water.
apps.spoken: Herb gardens flourish on sunny windowsills.
apps.writing: Use flourish for living things or communities that grow strong.

cloze.s: With plenty of sunlight and fresh water, the wildflowers began to ___ across the meadow.

cloze2.s: Fish ___ in the cool, clean stream, and their numbers rise every spring.

misuse.s: The plant flourished so badly that its leaves turned brown and fell off.
misuse.why: To flourish is to grow well; brown, falling leaves show the plant was not doing well.

visual.alt: A tall sunflower under a bright sun.

words.def: A substance that living things need to grow and stay healthy.
words.ex: Plants take in nutrients such as nitrogen from the soil through their roots.
words.ex2: Milk gives children calcium, a nutrient that helps build strong bones.
words.nonExample: A pile of plain gravel gives plants no nutrients.

apps.academic: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil so plants can use them again.
apps.writing: Use nutrient for a specific substance that feeds plants or animals.

cloze.s: Calcium is a ___ that growing bones need, and milk and cheese are good sources of it.

cloze2.s: Roots absorb water and ___ from the soil, which the plant uses to build leaves and stems.

misuse.s: A nutrient is a poison that makes plants wilt and die.
misuse.why: A nutrient helps living things grow; it is not a poison.

passage.title: Wolves, Willows, and a River
paras: Yellowstone National Park shows how all living things are connected. By the 1920s, wolves, the park's top predator, had been hunted out of the area. Without them, the number of elk, their main prey, grew. Hungry elk ate so many young willow trees along the rivers that few were left.
Willow roots hold soil in place. As the willows began to dwindle, erosion wore away some riverbanks, and fewer beavers and songbirds could find food and shelter.

In 1995, wolves were brought back. Many scientists think that, along with weather and hunting outside the park, the wolves helped change where and how elk feed. In some places, young willows began to flourish again, their roots slowed erosion, and beavers returned.

Wolves help in another way. Foxes, eagles, and bears eat what a wolf leaves behind, and the rest begins to decompose. This returns nutrients to the soil and makes the ground more fertile. Rangers also watch for human harm: if trash or chemicals pollute a stream, or fuel leaks contaminate it, animals that drink there can get sick.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "dwindle" means to
qs.why: The willows were being eaten and few were left, so dwindle means to become fewer little by little.

qs.q: Why did erosion increase along the rivers after the willows declined?
choices: Willow roots no longer held the soil in place.
qs.why: The first sentence of paragraph 2 says willow roots hold soil in place, so fewer willows meant less protection.

qs.q: Which sentence shows that scientists are careful about what caused the changes?
choices: Hungry elk ate so many young willow trees that few were left.
Foxes, eagles, and bears eat what a wolf leaves behind.
Rangers also watch for human harm.
Many scientists think that, along with weather and hunting outside the park, the wolves helped change where elk feed.
qs.why: The sentence names other possible causes and says the wolves helped, which is careful wording.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Changing one part of a community can affect many other living things.
Willow trees grow only near rivers.
Elk are the most important animals in the park.
qs.why: Each paragraph shows how removing or adding wolves affects plants, riverbanks, and other animals.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten science and environment words (three Tier 3 terms: predator, prey, erosion), read a science passage about wolves, willows, and a river, and write short explanations that use cause and effect. They connect the words to proof and trustworthy sources.

notes.va.predator.n: Name the Tier 3 term plainly and pair it with prey on a two-column chart. Ask what each animal gets: food or safety.
notes.va.prey.n: A noun in this unit. Students may know prey as a verb in 'prey on'; keep to the noun. Ask for three examples of prey from the passage and from their own science notes.
notes.va.erosion.n: Tier 3. Show a model with a tray of soil and a pour of water. Distinguish erosion (wearing away and moving) from weathering (breaking down); keep weathering for grade 6.
notes.va.fertile.adj: Link to fertilizer and fertility. Ask which one makes land fertile and how nutrients are involved.
notes.va.contaminate.v: A specific harmful thing gets into something: contaminate a well, a sample, food. Compare with pollute, which is broader.
notes.va.pollute.v: Broader harm to air, water, or land. Pair with contaminate and ask students to choose between them for three given situations.
notes.va.decompose.v: de- (undo) + compose. Connect to decomposers (fungi, bacteria). Plastic and glass take a very long time; ask why.
notes.va.dwindle.v: A slow, steady fall. Contrast with 'vanish', which is sudden. Use a graph with a falling line.
notes.va.flourish.v: Not just 'grow': grow well. Ask what conditions make something flourish.
notes.va.nutrient.n: Specific substances: nitrogen for plants, calcium for bones. Do not reduce to 'food'. Connect to fertile and decompose.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says elk grew in number and ate many willows. Willow roots hold soil, so fewer willows means more erosion. That is cause and effect. I can use predator and prey to start: no predator, so more prey, so fewer willows, so more erosion.'
discuss: What other community change could affect many living things?
Which source on a science topic would be most trustworthy, and what proof would you look for?
misconceptions: A predator is always large or scary.
Erosion and weathering are the same thing.
Pollute and contaminate always mean exactly the same thing.
extend: Draw a food web with at least five living things and label the predator, the prey, and the decomposer.
Do a mini investigation: place soil in two trays, one with grass and one bare, and pour water to compare erosion.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Two days later, revisit with a quick sort: who eats whom, what happens to land, what harms nature. Connect proof and trustworthy to the passage claims, and use microscope when discussing how decomposers are studied.

needsReview: Facts: wolves were removed from Yellowstone by the 1920s and reintroduced in 1995; effects on elk, willows, beavers, and nutrient return are described with hedged wording ('many scientists think'). Verify against a current source before publication.
Spanish glosses (depredador, presa, menguar, prosperar, contaminar, contaminar el ambiente) not reviewed by a native speaker; contaminate and pollute share one Spanish verb in common use.
Sense boundary: prey is taught only as a noun; the verb sense (prey on) is left to later grades.
Erosion is taught without weathering; confirm the teacher note matches the science curriculum used.
